name: Cirrus
description: Thin, wispy streaks made of ice crystals, often called 'mare's tails.' They're the highest clouds in our sky and usually mean fair weather, though they can signal a change coming in the next day or so.
fun_fact: Cirrus clouds are made almost entirely of ice crystals because it's so cold at their altitude, even in summer.

name: Cirrostratus
description: A thin, sheet-like veil of ice-crystal cloud that often covers the whole sky, giving it a slightly hazy, milky look.
fun_fact: Cirrostratus is what creates the halo you sometimes see around the sun or moon, caused by light bending through its ice crystals.

name: Cirrocumulus
description: Small, white, rippled patches high in the sky, often arranged in rows, giving the sky a dappled or 'fish scale' look.
fun_fact: A sky full of cirrocumulus is nicknamed a 'mackerel sky' because the pattern resembles fish scales.

name: Altocumulus
description: Grayish-white patches or rolls of cloud, usually appearing in groups, with parts of the cloud often more shaded than others.
fun_fact: Altocumulus clouds appearing on a warm, humid summer morning can be a sign of thunderstorms later that day.

name: Altostratus
description: A gray or blue-gray sheet covering all or most of the sky, thin enough that the sun may appear as a dim disk behind it.
fun_fact: Altostratus often shows up ahead of a warm front and can thicken into nimbostratus as steady rain approaches.

name: Nimbostratus
description: A thick, dark gray, featureless layer of cloud that blocks out the sun almost entirely and produces continuous, steady rain or snow.
fun_fact: The name comes from the Latin 'nimbus' (rain) and 'stratus' (layer) — it's the classic all-day rainy-sky cloud.

name: Stratus
description: A flat, featureless gray layer that often blankets the entire sky, similar to fog that doesn't quite reach the ground.
fun_fact: Stratus clouds are essentially fog that has lifted slightly off the ground.

name: Stratocumulus
description: Large, lumpy, rounded clouds in patches or rows with some blue sky visible between them, one of the most common cloud types worldwide.
fun_fact: Stratocumulus is the most commonly observed cloud type on Earth, covering roughly a fifth of the planet's surface at any given time.

name: Cumulus
description: Puffy, white, cotton-ball-shaped clouds with flat bottoms and rounded tops, the classic 'fair weather' cloud kids draw in pictures.
fun_fact: A single cumulus cloud can weigh over a million pounds, but it still floats because that weight is spread across a huge volume of air only slightly denser than its surroundings.

name: Cumulonimbus
altitude_range: Low-level base, extending to high-level (surface-60,000+ ft)
description: Towering, anvil-shaped storm clouds that can stretch from near the ground into the upper atmosphere, producing thunder, lightning, heavy rain, and sometimes hail.
fun_fact: Cumulonimbus is the only cloud type that can produce hail, tornadoes, and lightning, and its flattened top is called an 'anvil.'
